blocks.text: Once you can filter a DataFrame down to the rows you care about, the next natural question is what order to look at them in. Maybe you want the highest spending customers first, or a leaderboard ranked by score, or your rows back in their original chronological order after some earlier operation scrambled everything. Sorting is how you answer all of that, and pandas gives you a genuinely small toolkit that covers almost every real situation.

blocks.alt: sort_values in ascending order by default versus descending with ascending set to False
blocks.caption: The single most common sorting call you will write, in both directions.

blocks.text: sort_values() sorts your DataFrame's rows by the values in one column. Ascending order is the default.
Pass a list of column names instead of a single one, and the first column becomes the primary sort key. Any ties in the first column get broken by the second column, and so on down the list.

blocks.alt: Sorting by department as the primary key and salary as the tiebreaker within each department
blocks.caption: Rows land grouped by department first, then ordered by salary inside each group.

blocks.text: You are not stuck with the same ascending or descending direction for every column in a multi column sort. Pass a matching list of booleans to ascending, one entry per sort column.

blocks.alt: Sorting department ascending while salary sorts descending within each department
blocks.caption: Alphabetical departments, but highest earners first within each one.

blocks.text: sort_index() sorts rows by their index labels rather than by any column's values. This comes up after operations that leave your rows in a scrambled order, or when you specifically want a date indexed DataFrame back in chronological order.

blocks.alt: sort_index putting rows back into order by their row labels rather than by any column value
blocks.caption: Useful after a groupby or a filter leaves your index in a different order than you expect.

blocks.text: NaN does not sort the way you might expect from a normal comparison, since it is not really comparable to anything. The na_position parameter lets you control whether missing values end up at the beginning or the end of the sorted result, rather than leaving it to chance.

blocks.alt: NaN values pushed to the end versus the beginning depending on na_position
blocks.caption: Without setting this explicitly, NaN placement can surprise you.

blocks.title: NaN needs an explicit position
blocks.content: By default na_position is last, but do not assume that everywhere, especially when you are chaining sorts across columns with mixed missingness. Set it explicitly when it matters.

blocks.text: Like most pandas methods, sort_values() and sort_index() accept an inplace=True option that mutates the DataFrame directly instead of returning a new one. Modern pandas usage generally prefers reassigning the result instead, since it keeps your code easier to trace and avoids surprising side effects on a DataFrame another part of your code might still be relying on.
6. Top N and Bottom N with nlargest and nsmallest

If all you actually want is the top or bottom few rows by some column, sorting the entire DataFrame just to slice off the first few rows wastes work. nlargest() and nsmallest() get you there directly.

blocks.alt: nlargest pulling the top 5 rows by a column without sorting the whole DataFrame
blocks.caption: Skips sorting the millions of rows you were never going to look at anyway.

blocks.alt: nsmallest as the mirror image, pulling the bottom N rows instead
blocks.caption: Same idea, opposite direction.

blocks.alt: sort_values followed by head sorting everything first, versus nlargest going straight to the answer
blocks.caption: On a large DataFrame this difference is not just style, it is real wasted work.

blocks.title: Prefer nlargest/nsmallest for top N tasks
blocks.content: sort_values(...).head(5) works, but it sorts every single row first even though you only wanted 5. nlargest/nsmallest are built specifically for this and skip that wasted work.

blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: Top Orders and a Leaderboard
Finding the five highest value orders is a one liner with nlargest.

blocks.alt: The five highest value orders pulled directly from the orders DataFrame
blocks.caption: One call, no intermediate sort step.

blocks.text: A leaderboard is a great example of multi column sorting with mixed directions. Sort by score descending as the primary key, and break ties with an earlier submission timestamp ascending, so whoever got the same score in first wins the tie.

blocks.alt: A leaderboard sorted by score descending with ties broken by an earlier submission timestamp ascending
blocks.caption: Highest score wins. If two people tie, whoever submitted first wins the tiebreak.

items: sort_values() sorts by one or more column values, ascending by default.
A list of columns creates a primary key plus tiebreakers, each with its own optional direction.
sort_index() sorts by row labels instead of column values.
Set na_position explicitly when missing values are present and their placement matters.
Prefer reassigning the result over inplace=True.
nlargest/nsmallest beat sort_values().head() for a top N task, since they skip sorting rows you never needed.
